title: Unit 09: Good-bye Mr. Chips Part 3 (Chapters 13–18: WW1, Linford, Farewell)
subject: english-12

questions.question: In 1916, during the dark days of World War I, why did Headmaster Chatteris visit Mr. Chips at Mrs. Wickett's cottage?

options.A: To invite him to tea in London
options.B: To beg Chips to come out of retirement and return to Brookfield to teach Latin and help manage the school during a severe wartime staff shortage
options.D: To inform him that Brookfield was being closed down

questions.explanation: Young masters had enlisted to fight in France, replacements were incompetent or elderly, and Chatteris was dying of diabetes and desperate for Chips' help.

questions.question: What was Chips' immediate response to Chatteris' plea for help in 1916?

options.A: He agreed immediately with quiet, patriotic joy, putting on his old tattered gown and returning to the classroom the very next morning.
options.B: He refused, claiming his health was too fragile.
options.C: He demanded double his old salary.
options.D: He advised Chatteris to hire German teachers.

questions.explanation: Chips was thrilled to be useful again; he stepped back into his old post with renewed youthful vigor and devotion.

questions.question: When Chatteris succumbed to his illness in April 1917, what major responsibility fell upon Mr. Chips?

options.A: He was appointed Acting Headmaster of Brookfield for the duration of the war.
options.B: He was conscripted into the trench infantry.
options.C: He was elected Member of Parliament.
options.D: He was sent to France as an army chaplain.

questions.explanation: The governors unanimously asked Chips to take the reins as Acting Headmaster, leading Brookfield through the hardest year of the Great War.

questions.question: What heartbreaking duty did Mr. Chips perform every Sunday in chapel during the war years?

options.A: Reading aloud the long lists of former Brookfield boys who had been killed in action on the battlefields of Flanders and Gallipoli
options.B: Delivering military recruitment speeches
options.D: Punishing boys who refused to drill

questions.explanation: Week after week, Chips stood at the chapel lectern reading the names of fallen soldiers, remembering each boy's face, smile, and mischief.

questions.question: Whose name did Chips bravely read aloud in chapel among the war dead, despite fierce wartime anti-German hysteria?

options.A: Max Staefel, the former German master who had taught at Brookfield and was killed fighting on the Western Front
options.B: Kaiser Wilhelm II

questions.explanation: Chips demonstrated supreme Christian humanity by honoring Max Staefel, a gentle former colleague who died fighting on the German side.

questions.question: What extraordinary incident occurred in Big Hall during an air raid by German Zeppelins/Gothas in 1918?

options.A: The school was destroyed and everyone died.
options.B: While bombs shook the building and explosions echoed outside, Chips calmly continued his Latin class, quipping: 'Let us translate Caesar; these modern affairs are mere ephemera!'
options.C: Chips ran into the forest in panic.
options.D: The boys captured an enemy parachute.

questions.explanation: Chips' serene, unflinching composure kept the frightened boys steady as he playfully parsed Latin grammar during the bombardment.

questions.question: On what historic day did World War I finally conclude, coinciding with a joyous whole-holiday at Brookfield?

options.A: 11 November 1918 (Armistice Day)
options.B: 4 August 1914

questions.explanation: On 11 November 1918, the guns fell silent on the Western Front, and Chips stepped down from his wartime headmastership into final retirement.

questions.question: In Chapter 18, on a cold, foggy afternoon in November 1933, who came to visit Mr. Chips at Mrs. Wickett's?

options.A: Linford, a new boy at Brookfield from Shropshire, sent by mischief-makers as a prank to tea with old Chips
options.B: The ghost of Katherine

questions.explanation: Young Linford was tricked by older boys into believing Chips had invited him; Chips warmly welcomed the lad, fed him tea and walnut cake, and chatted happily.

questions.question: What memorable words did young Linford say as he stepped out into the foggy dusk, echoing Katherine's words thirty-seven years earlier?

options.A: 'Good-bye, Mr. Chips!'
options.B: 'Thank you for the tea, sir!'

questions.explanation: As the boy waved through the mist, he called out: 'Good-bye, Mr. Chips!' bringing tears of nostalgic memory to Chips' eyes.

questions.question: What happened to Mr. Chips shortly after young Linford's visit?

options.A: He collapsed from a sudden fainting spell and was carried to his bed, drifting into a peaceful final coma.
options.B: He flew in an airplane to London.
options.C: He decided to teach another ten years.

questions.explanation: Chips fainted by his chair, and Mrs. Wickett and Dr. Merivale found him and placed him in bed for his final transition.

questions.question: Around Chips' deathbed, who were gathered speaking in hushed whispers?

options.A: Dr. Merivale, Mrs. Wickett, and the new young Headmaster Cartwright
options.B: The King and Queen of England

questions.explanation: His loyal doctor, housekeeper, and the school headmaster stood quietly watching over his fading breath.

questions.question: What did Headmaster Cartwright whisper about Chips that prompted the dying old master to open his eyes for the last time?

options.A: 'It's a pity... a great pity he never had any children.'
options.B: 'He was the worst teacher Brookfield ever had.'

questions.explanation: Cartwright whispered that it was sad Chips was a childless bachelor, not knowing of his tragic past with Katherine.

questions.question: What sublime response did Mr. Chips summon his last ounce of strength to utter from his deathbed?

options.A: 'Yes, I have children... thousands of them... thousands of them... and all of them boys!'
options.B: 'I want to go back to Great Gable.'

questions.explanation: In one of the most moving climaxes in literature, Chips declared that every boy who ever passed through Brookfield was his own beloved child.

questions.question: In his final moments as his eyes closed forever, what did Chips see drifting in his mind?

options.A: A vast procession of thousands of young faces, smiling, calling out their names, answering roll-call in the eternal hall of memory
options.B: Cold empty space and dying stars

questions.explanation: He saw the luminous faces of all his Brookfield boys, chanting call-over in happy unison as he fell into gentle, eternal sleep.

questions.question: In what year did Mr. Chips pass away?

options.A: November 1933, at the age of eighty-five

questions.explanation: Chips died peacefully in November 1933, having lived eighty-five rich, honorable, and beloved years.

questions.question: What did Chips do with his modest financial savings in his last will and testament?

options.A: He left a portion to Mrs. Wickett and established an open scholarship fund for needy boys at Brookfield School.
options.B: He left everything to the British Treasury.
options.C: He bought gold bullion to bury in the woods.
options.D: He gave it all to foreign banks.

questions.explanation: Even in death, Chips ensured that his modest wealth benefited his loyal landlady and supported impoverished scholars at Brookfield.

questions.question: Why is the character of Max Staefel so central to James Hilton's humanist theme?

options.A: It shows that true human decency transcends nationalism, xenophobia, and wartime hatred.
options.B: It proves that German teachers were better than English teachers.
options.C: It was a historical critique of the Kaiser.
options.D: It showed that languages should not be taught in war.

questions.explanation: Honoring Staefel exemplified Chips' refusal to succumb to blind wartime prejudice, recognizing that ordinary people on both sides were victims of war.

questions.question: What did the doctor mean when he said Chips died of 'old age'?

options.A: He suffered from no disease or pain; his vital clock simply wound down peacefully like a natural sunset.
options.B: He had contracted influenza.

questions.explanation: Chips suffered from no organic illness; his gentle, tired heart simply ceased beating after a full, completed life.

questions.question: What is the tone of the final chapter of 'Good-bye, Mr. Chips'?

options.A: Profoundly moving, serene, nostalgic, and triumphant in its celebration of a life dedicated to youth
options.B: Angry and bitter at the cruelty of death

questions.explanation: The conclusion is filled with spiritual dignity, quiet beauty, and tears of profound fulfillment.

questions.question: Identify the literary device used in: 'The bells of Brookfield were the heartbeat of his peaceful old age.'

options.A: Metaphor
options.B: Simile

questions.explanation: Equating the school bells directly to the heartbeat of his life is a lyrical metaphor.

questions.question: What happened to the boys Chips taught during his wartime headmastership?

options.A: They felt a unique, tender devotion toward him because his presence provided stability in a terrifying, chaotic world.
options.B: They mutinied against his Latin tests.
options.C: They all transferred to military schools.

questions.explanation: To young boys with brothers and fathers dying at the front, old Chips was a comforting rock of grandfatherly peace and sanity.

questions.question: What was the significance of Linford's visit to Chips?

options.A: It completed the circle of his life: his final living conversation was with a lonely young schoolboy who needed comfort and warmth.
options.B: Linford came to arrest him.

questions.explanation: Hilton poignantly bookends Chips' career with an innocent schoolboy, proving that Chips' ministry of love continued to his final breath.

questions.question: What is the synonym of 'poignant' as used to describe Chips' deathbed scene?

options.A: Deeply moving, touching, and evoking a keen sense of sadness and beauty
options.B: Boring and repetitive

questions.explanation: 'Poignant' means evoking a keen sense of sadness, regret, or tender emotional resonance.

questions.question: What was Chatteris' cause of death during the war?

options.A: Diabetes and physical overwork at the age of forty-one
options.B: Killed by a bomb in London

questions.explanation: Chatteris worked himself to death trying to keep Brookfield running while suffering from severe diabetes.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence:

options.A: Hardly had Chips entered the hall when the boys rose to their feet.
options.B: Hardly had Chips entered the hall than the boys rose to their feet.
options.C: Hardly Chips had entered the hall when the boys rose to their feet.
options.D: Hardly did Chips entered the hall when the boys rose.

questions.explanation: Negative adverbial inversion: 'Hardly had + subject + V3 ... when' is the correct correlative construction.

questions.question: What did Chips whisper right before he passed into his final sleep?

options.A: He smiled, murmured the names of boys, and sighed peacefully.
options.B: He cried out in fear.
options.C: He asked for Dr. Merivale's medicine.
options.D: He complained of the cold weather.

questions.explanation: Hilton writes that Chips smiled a contented smile, his lips moving gently with the names of his beloved boys.

questions.question: What did the author James Hilton base the character of Mr. Chips upon in real life?

options.A: His own father, John Hilton (a dedicated schoolmaster), and his former Latin master, W.H. Balgarnie of The Leys School, Cambridge
options.B: Winston Churchill

questions.explanation: Hilton drew inspiration from his schoolmaster father and his beloved Latin teacher W.H. Balgarnie, who taught at The Leys for over fifty years.

questions.question: Why did Chips say he was glad he lived into the 1930s?

options.A: Because he could watch airplanes and see a new generation carrying forward the noble spirit of England
options.B: Because television was invented

questions.explanation: Chips maintained an open, gentle heart toward the modern era, seeing the eternal goodness of youth in each new decade.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the idiom 'to pass away'?

options.A: To walk across a bridge
options.B: To die peacefully (a gentle euphemism)

questions.explanation: 'Pass away' is the standard polite euphemism for dying.

questions.question: What did Cartwright mean when he said: 'He was Brookfield, and Brookfield was him'?

options.A: Chips had become the living embodiment of the school's history, soul, and moral traditions.
options.B: Chips legally owned the land.
options.C: The school was going to be demolished.
options.D: Chips was the only master left.

questions.explanation: Chips and Brookfield were inseparable in spirit; sixty-three years of association made him the school's immortal avatar.

questions.question: Identify the grammatical role of 'Good-bye' in the title 'Good-bye, Mr. Chips':

options.A: Interjection used as a valediction/farewell
options.B: Transitive verb

questions.explanation: 'Good-bye' is an interjection expressing farewell, derived from the archaic phrase 'God be with ye'.

questions.question: What was the weather like on the day young Linford visited Mr. Chips?

options.A: A cold, damp, yellow autumn fog enveloping the village and school
options.B: A bright tropical heatwave
options.C: A fierce blizzard with five feet of snow

questions.explanation: Hilton sets the poignant closing scene in an atmospheric November dusk shrouded in cold English autumn fog.

questions.question: What is the antonym of 'ephemeral' as used by Chips during the air raid ('these modern affairs are mere ephemera')?

options.A: Transient
options.B: Eternal / Enduring / Permanent

questions.explanation: 'Ephemeral' means lasting for a very short time; its opposite is enduring, permanent, or eternal.

questions.question: What was the final sound that echoed across the quiet evening as Chips closed his eyes?

options.A: The chimes of the Brookfield chapel bell ringing for lights-out
options.B: The whistle of a steam train

questions.explanation: The distant, comforting tones of the Brookfield bell tolled across the autumn air, marking the gentle close of a noble life.

questions.question: What is the supreme moral message of James Hilton's masterpiece 'Good-bye, Mr. Chips'?

options.A: That a modest life dedicated quietly, lovingly, and faithfully to teaching, kindness, and human connection leaves an eternal, glorious monument in the hearts of others
options.B: That only military conquests make a man great
options.C: That Latin is the only subject worth learning
options.D: That wealth is the sole measure of human success

questions.explanation: Hilton's enduring novel proves that quiet goodness, dedication to youth, and loving kindness outshine all the noisy vanity of the world.
